note:
God rules and delivers His people before the time of the monarchy. He does so by raising up Samuel (chs. 1–3), intervening directly against the Philistines (4:1–7:1), and giving Samuel victory over the Philistines (7:2–17).

**1:1 a certain man.** This expression and the accompanying genealogy suggest that Elkanah is a man of standing. The reference to a barren wife (v. 2) resembles the introduction to the birth of Samson (Judg. 13:2).

**Ramathaim-zophim.** Possibly meaning “twin heights,” the name occurs only here in the OT. It may be the same location as the NT Arimathea (northwest of Bethel). Samuel’s hometown is usually called Ramah, about five miles (8 km) north of Jerusalem (1:19; 2:11; 7:17; 8:4; 15:34; 19:18; 25:1).

**of Zuph.** “Zuph” is both a personal name (1 Chr. 6:35) and a territory (9:5).

**Ephrathite.** Ephraim is the place he is from, not necessarily the tribe of his ancestry (1 Chr. 6:16–30, 33–37).

Monogamy is God’s design for humanity (Gen. 2:18–25). Polygamy is first mentioned in Gen. 4:19. It is possibly recognized and regulated, though not endorsed, in Deut. 21:15–17, although this passage may address a situation in which a man remarries after the death of his first wife.

**no children.** Hannah is childless and is provoked by her fertile rival (vv. 6, 7). A barren but favored wife who receives a special offspring from Yahweh is not uncommon in the OT. See Gen. 18:1–15 (Sarah/Isaac); 25:21–26 (Rebekah/Esau and Jacob); 30:22–24 (Rachel/Joseph); and Judg. 13:2–5 (Manoah’s wife/Samson). In the NT, see Luke 1:5–25 (Elizabeth/John).

verse_quote: this man used to go up.
note:
Perhaps he observes “the yearly feast of the LORD at Shiloh” (Judg. 21:19), or perhaps he goes for a family ceremony (20:6). In the Pentateuch, reference is made to three annual pilgrim feasts (Ex. 23:14–17; 34:18–23; Deut. 16:1–17).

**of hosts.** This title occurs here for the first time in the OT. “LORD” denotes the personal name of the God of Israel (Heb. _Yahweh_). The Hebrew word translated “hosts” can also be rendered as “armies.” Depending on the context, this includes the hosts of Israel (17:45), the cosmic hosts or celestial bodies (Deut. 4:19), and the angelic hosts (Josh. 5:14). As a whole, the title expresses the Lord’s sovereignty over all earthly and heavenly powers.

**Shiloh.** Halfway between Shechem and Bethel, Shiloh (modern Seilun) is an important Israelite religious center in the period before the monarchy (Josh. 18:1; Judg. 21:19). The sanctuary there (Jer. 7:12), and perhaps more of it, may have been destroyed by the Philistines after the battle of Aphek (4:1–11). Excavations have revealed that Shiloh was a thriving town during the early Iron Age.

**Eli.** As with some other well-known people in the OT (Joshua, Ex. 17:9; and Jonathan, 1 Sam. 13:2), Eli is first introduced by name only.

The Hebrew is difficult but has usually been interpreted as an especially honorable portion or perhaps a double portion. Elkanah’s attempts to lessen Hannah’s sorrow by expressing his love for her (v. 8) are ineffective.

**the** LORD **had closed her womb.** Hannah’s barrenness comes not by chance or as a form of punishment (2 Sam. 6:23) but is under the Lord’s sovereign control.
See note on 1:2.

Hannah refuses to eat until the Lord answers her prayer; cf. David’s actions in 2 Sam. 12:16–20 and Saul’s in 1 Sam. 28:23–25. In the NT, fasting often accompanies serious dealings with the Lord (Acts 13:2, 3; 14:23).

The mention of a “doorpost” here and “doors” in 3:15, as well as sleeping quarters in 3:2, 3, may suggest a more permanent structure than the tent of Moses’s time. Other designations for the structure in Samuel are “the house of the LORD” (v. 7; 3:15) and “the tent of meeting” (2:22). From 2 Sam. 7:6 it is clear that in the era before the time of David, the tabernacle or temple is a tent and not a permanent structure.

On the making of vows by married women and the husbands’ responsibility to confirm or nullify, see Num. 30:6–15.

**remember me.** Hannah asks not simply for the Lord to keep her in mind but for Him to do something special to help her.

**no razor.** Hannah’s vow reflects elements of the Nazirite vow (Num. 6:1–21), which includes abstaining from grapes or anything made from grapes, not cutting the hair, and avoiding all contact with dead bodies. While such vows are generally made for a limited period of time, Hannah’s is for “all the days” of her son’s life (cf. Judg. 13:5 note).

Eli’s conclusion that Hannah is drunk is an unsettling element in the narrative because it suggests that he is unfamiliar with fervency in prayer. Drunkenness in the tabernacle precincts is a severe offense, particularly priests, who are to be executed for ministering in such a condition (Lev. 10:9).
Lit. a “daughter of Belial,” which is an idiom for a worthless person. The word “Belial” is later used of Eli’s own sons (2:12).

verse_quote: her face was no longer sad.
note: Hannah’s actions in response to the benediction of v. 17 give evidence of her belief.

Various meanings of the name “Samuel” have been suggested, including “heard by God,” “he who is from God,” “name of God,” and even “son of God” (as one “given” or “promised” by God). Regardless of the linguistic etymology, “heard of God” is the folk etymology: Hannah asked and her prayer was heard by God. “Saul” is also from the Hebrew verb “to ask” (8:10 note).
See Lev. 7:16 and note.
In the ancient Near East a child was weaned later than is customary today. Weaning may also have been celebrated with a feast (Gen. 21:8).
“Your word” is also a plausible translation here. Elkanah, as Hannah’s husband (1:11 note), invokes the Lord’s assistance in Hannah’s fulfillment of her vow.
According to Num. 15:8–10, the fulfillment of a vow is to be accompanied by an offering of a young bull, fine flour, and wine. Hannah brings all three but in larger measure than required.

Her prayer for a son having been answered, Hannah offers a jubilant song of thanksgiving. Focusing on the Lord’s sovereignty and the exaltation of the humble, Hannah anticipates the major themes of the books of Samuel. The same themes of sovereignty, grace, and deliverance are reiterated in David’s song of thanksgiving near the end of 2 Samuel (ch. 22). The two songs provide a poetic frame for 1 and 2 Samuel. Mary’s briefer song of praise (the Magnificat, Luke 1:46–55) seems to be modeled on Hannah’s. The settings of the two stories are similar: a childless woman receives God’s intervention in the birth of a son. Both descendants grow up to deliver their people. Both songs open with rejoicing in the Lord’s deliverance (v. 1; Luke 1:46–48), extol the Lord’s uniqueness and holiness (v. 2; Luke 1:49, 50), condemn proud boasting (v. 3; Luke 1:51), point to reversals of human fortune as the result of interventions by the sovereign Lord (vv. 4–8; Luke 1:52, 53), and express the Lord’s faithful care for His own (v. 9; Luke 1:54, 55). Hannah’s song concludes with the assertion that the Lord Himself will give strength to His king, His anointed (vv. 9–10).

**2:1 horn.** It is God who exalts the strength of the righteous but cuts off the strength of the wicked (Ps. 75:10).

As a metaphor for God, this term is concentrated in poetic passages such as the song of Moses in Deut. 32; the song of David in 2 Sam. 22; Psalms; and Isaiah. The metaphor suggests God’s strength and sovereignty and the security of those who trust in Him. Here the focus is on the uniqueness of the one true God as opposed to false sources of security (cf. false gods, also called “rock,” in Deut. 32:31, 37; Is. 44:8).
The number seven represents ideal completeness (see Ruth 4:15).

Hannah’s acknowledgment of the actions of the Lord takes the form of four merisms. A merism is a figure of speech in which two opposite terms signify inclusiveness. As these words express, the Lord is sovereign over all things.

Hannah’s reference to God’s raising the poor to sit with princes highlights an important theme in the books of Samuel. Those who display humility are promoted to king. However, the reverse is also true. Arrogance and pride are important factors in the divine rejection of Saul.

verse_quote: for not by might shall a man prevail.
note: The subsequent narratives confirm that it is not physical prowess but God’s presence that brings success. In the ark narrative of chs. 4–6, the Lord makes His hand felt by the Philistines without the assistance of human agents (5:6). Other such examples are the Lord’s victory through Samuel in ch. 7; the contrasting successes of Saul and Jonathan in chs. 13, 14; the choice of David, the youngest of Jesse’s sons, in ch. 16; and David’s victory over Goliath in ch. 17.

The reference to the Lord’s king here points forward to the central event of the books of Samuel, namely, the institution of a monarchy, and implies that the idea of kingship, properly conceived, is not wrong. That Israel will have a king is anticipated in various places in the Pentateuch (Gen. 49:10; Num. 24:7, 17–19; Deut. 17:14–20).

**exalt the horn.** The horn is a symbol of power that derives from the picture of the strength of a goring animal such as a bull (v. 1 and note).

**his anointed.** Numerous objects and persons were subject to religious anointing in ancient Israel (Ex. 30:22–33), but it was the king ultimately who had the title of the “Lord’s anointed” or simply “the anointed.” Persons chosen for divine service were anointed to signify their calling and their authority to perform the service. Anointing also signified that God would give them the help they needed. References to the king as the Lord’s anointed are prevalent in the books of Samuel (v. 35; 12:3, 5; 16:6; 24:6) and Psalms (2:2; 18:50). The present passage is the first reference to a king of Israel as God’s anointed, though the idea of anointing a king is found in Jotham’s fable (Judg. 9:8, 15). The English word “messiah” comes from the Hebrew word meaning “anointed.” In the NT, “Christ” translates the Greek word _Christos,_ also meaning “anointed.”

This Hebrew phrase (lit. “sons of Belial”) connotes vile persons. It is used of those who incite to idolatry (Deut. 13:13) or insurrection (10:27; 2 Sam. 16:7; 20:1); the sexually immoral (Judg. 19:22); and liars (1 Kin. 21:10, 13). The phrase is appropriately applied to Eli’s sons.

**did not know.** This is the heart of the problem. Use of the verb “know” here and in 3:7 sets up an ironic contrast between Eli’s sons and Samuel (3:7 note).

The practice described in vv. 13, 14 is different from the prescriptions of Lev. 7:28–36 and Deut. 18:3. The greed of the sons of Eli has caused the people to treat “the offering of the LORD with contempt” (v. 17).

Since the time of Abel’s offering of the fat of the firstborn of his flock (Gen. 4:4), the fat portion was considered to be the best, and as such, to belong to the Lord. The priests had the duty of burning the fat on the altar as an offering to the Lord (Lev. 3:16; 7:31). Like blood, the fat was strictly forbidden for human consumption, and anyone who ate it would be expelled from the people (Lev. 3:17; 7:23–25).

The behavior of Samuel, who ministers faithfully before the Lord, and also of Eli, who regularly blesses Elkanah and his wife (v. 20), is in sharp contrast to the abuses of Eli’s sons.

**linen ephod.** A short inner garment of some sort, and associated with priestly service (22:18), the linen ephod is worn also by King David when he brought the ark to Jerusalem (2 Sam. 6:14). See also 2:28 and note.
An outer garment to be worn over the linen ephod.
Eli’s words recall those of Hannah in 1:27, 28. Both “petition” and “asked” in Hebrew derive from the same word as the name “Saul” (1:20 note).
LORD **.** Or “with the LORD.” The same Hebrew expression is used in v. 26.

Again, as at v. 12, the focus shifts from the boy Samuel to the house of Eli.

**kept hearing.** Eli must be told about what he should already observe and control. But his offenses run much deeper than mere inattentiveness (v. 29).

**lay with the women.** On the “tent of meeting,” see note on 1:9; on “the women who were serving,” see Ex. 38:8. Though explicitly condemned by the law (Deut. 23:17, 18), religious prostitution was practiced by the Canaanites and posed a constant danger to the Israelites (1 Kin. 15:12; 2 Kin. 23:7; Hos. 4:14).

Eli’s point is that while there may be some mediation of disputes between people, when someone offends God there is no one who can intervene. Eli’s sons have sinned first and foremost against the Lord (v. 17), and they seal their doom by refusing to hear Eli’s warning.

**it was the will of the** LORD **to put them to death.** This clear statement of God’s sovereignty over the destiny of the wicked does not diminish people’s responsibility for their own actions.

LORD **.** The gravity of Eli’s sons’ refusal to listen to their father or God is emphasized by the striking contrast to Samuel, who grows in favor with God and people. The emphasis on Samuel’s growth as more than merely physical foreshadows a theme that is later developed in the contrasting portraits of Saul and David. The expression of v. 26 is used by Luke to describe the childhood of Jesus (Luke 2:52; see Prov. 3:4).

The words of the man of God to Eli exhibit features typical of prophetic judgment speeches. There is an accusation (expressed here through accusing questions that emphasize the contrast between the Lord’s grace and Eli’s disobedience) and an announcement of judgment confirmed by a sign. Other examples of prophetic speeches of this type are found in chs. 13; 15; and 2 Sam. 12:7–12.

**2:27 man of God.** In the OT this designation is used interchangeably with “prophet” (9:8–11; 1 Kin. 13:14–18; 2 Kin. 5:8; 6:10–12).

**house of your father ... in Egypt.** Although Eli’s genealogy is nowhere recorded in the OT, v. 28 implies that he is a descendant of Aaron. The assertion that the Lord revealed Himself and selected Eli’s house as far back as the period of Israelite servitude in Egypt underscores the gross ingratitude of the house of Eli.

Or perhaps “carry” an ephod. The ephod mentioned here is not the garment mentioned in v. 18 but the high-priestly ephod bearing the “breastpiece of judgment” and the “Urim and Thummim,” through which the ancient Israelites determine the Lord’s will (Ex. 28:4–30).

**gave ... my offerings.** Both in the OT (Num. 18:8; Deut. 18:1) and in the NT (1 Cor. 9:13, 14; 1 Tim. 5:17, 18), God provides for the support of those who are called to full-time ministry.

Though the offenses of his sons are more blatant, Eli himself does not escape blame. As father and high priest, he should confront his sons with more than words (vv. 23–25). His failure to take action amounts to honoring his sons above the Lord (v. 30). The Hebrew word for “honor” is key in the subsequent accounts of the fall of the family of Eli and the capture and return of the ark (chs. 4–7); see notes on 4:21; 6:5, 6.
That is, continually or indefinitely.

verse_quote: will not be an old man in your house.
note: The downfall of Eli’s house begins with the death of his sons (4:11) and himself (4:18). It continues with Saul’s massacre of the priests of Nob (22:17–19) and culminates in Solomon’s removal of Abiathar from the priesthood (1 Kin. 2:26, 27).

verse_quote: in distress you will look with envious eye.
note: The Hebrew is difficult, and parts of vv. 31, 32 are lacking in the Septuagint and the Dead Sea Scrolls.
Prophetic utterances are often confirmed by signs in the OT (2:27–36 note; cf. 10:7, 9; 1 Kin. 13:3, 5; 2 Kin. 19:29; 20:8, 9).

While the statement in 3:20 that Samuel is “established” as a prophet of the Lord suggests Samuel may be the fulfillment of this prediction, the clearer fulfillment comes in the person of Zadok, who serves as high priest alongside Abiathar under David (2 Sam. 8:17 note) and comes to preeminence under Solomon (1 Kin. 2:35). The descendants of Zadok hold the high priesthood from the time of Solomon to the time of Antiochus Epiphanes and the Maccabees (for details see Introduction to the Intertestamental Period).

**my anointed.** This is the second allusion in this chapter to the coming king (v. 10 note).
Prophetic judgments are characterized by a correspondence of crime and punishment. The hunger threatened in this verse corresponds to the greedy satisfaction described in vv. 12–27, 29.

This section describes the Lord’s call to Samuel to be a prophet.

**3:1 the word of the** LORD **was rare.** The Lord’s withholding His word is a sign of His displeasure (14:37; Ps. 74:9; Lam. 2:9; Amos 8:11, 12). Conversely, His communication to Samuel is a sign of favor.

**vision.** The Hebrew word often denotes an auditory encounter rather than a visual one. God’s revelation of His will is necessary for the well being of God’s people (Prov. 29:18).
Ironically, Eli has neither physical nor spiritual vision (cf. v. 1).

verse_quote: The lamp of God had not yet gone out.
note:
This notice may be simply a time reference (Ex. 27:20–21; Lev. 24:1–4). “Lamp” is used as a metaphor for guidance, blessing, proclamation, and revelation. In the context of 3:1, “the word of the LORD was rare in those days; there was no frequent vision,” “lamp” here probably refers to divine revelation. Though rare, divine revelation has not been snuffed out completely in Samuel’s era (see v. 21).

**temple.** See note on 1:9.

**ark of God.** Elsewhere called “the ark of the testimony” and “the ark of the covenant,” this chest of acacia wood overlaid with gold is described in Ex. 25:10–22. The Israelites consider this ark to be the footstool of the heavenly throne (1 Sam. 4:4). The ark is important in chs. 4–6 and again in 2 Sam. 6.

verse_quote: Samuel did not yet know the
note: LORD **.** The repetition of terminology from 2:12 about knowing God only emphasizes the contrast in meaning. Eli’s sons “did not know the LORD,” because they wickedly disregarded Him. Samuel is a child, and no revelation has yet come to him.

Eli’s slowness to recognize that God is calling Samuel recalls earlier instances of misperception (1:12–16) and unawareness (2:22 note), contributing to the reader’s impression of Eli as an aged priest whose eyes have grown dim (v. 2) in more ways than one.
The drama of the scene now becomes greatly heightened. The verb “stood” is occasionally used of God when He appears in a theophany (Gen. 18:2; 28:13; Num. 22:22).
See 2:27–36. The repetition to Samuel of the oracle against Eli confirms the oracle itself and establishes Samuel as a prophet of the Lord (v. 20).

If Eli’s sons are cursing God, they are committing an offense worthy of death (Lev. 24:15, 16).

**did not restrain them.** Eli, in view of his position as high priest, should be taking action to restrain his sons once verbal rebuke proves ineffective (2:29 note; 2 Sam. 13:21 note).

verse_quote: not be atoned for by sacrifice or offering forever.
note: While there is provision to atone for unintentional priestly sins (Lev. 4:1–12), the sins of Eli’s house are clearly acts of open defiance (Num. 15:30–31). They have scorned the normal means of atonement, namely, sacrifice and offering (2:17, 29).

LORD**. Let him do what seems good to him.** Eli confesses God’s right to rule in the affairs of people. His words establish a benchmark by which later characters in the narrative should be judged: Saul (20:30, 31) and David (2 Sam. 15:25, 26).

LORD **was with him.** From the perspective of the books of Samuel, God’s presence with someone makes the difference between success and failure (16:18; 18:12, 14, 28).

**let none of his words fall to the ground.** See 9:6. Samuel thus passed the test of a true prophet (Deut. 18:21, 22).

verse_quote: Dan to Beersheba ... prophet of the
note: LORD **.** Dan is the northernmost city in the Promised Land and Beersheba the southernmost, so the phrase “Dan to Beersheba” is a colloquial way to refer to all Israel (cf. 2 Sam. 3:10; 17:11; 24:15; 1 Kin. 4:25). While Samuel’s responsibilities as judge take him on a circuit of the central hill country (7:15–17), his reputation as a prophet spreads throughout “all Israel.”
See note on 1:3.

verse_quote: the word of Samuel came to all Israel.
note:
The episode that began with a notice of the rarity of the word of the Lord (3:1) concludes with a notice of the change brought by the selection of Samuel to be “a prophet of the LORD” (3:20 and note).

**Philistines.** The Philistines are one of the “Sea Peoples” named in Egyptian texts from the time of Rameses III. By the time of the judges (Judg. 3:31; 13–16), the Philistines had settled along the coastlands of southern Canaan in a league of five cities: Ashdod, Ashkelon, Ekron, Gath, and Gaza (6:17; Judg. 3:3). The Philistines often tried to expand their territory, and in the time of Samuel and the early monarchy they came in direct conflict with the Israelites to the north and east. During the rule of Samson, the last judge, the Philistines were a thorn in Israel’s side (Judg. 15:20).

**Ebenezer.** This may be an archaeological site about two miles (3 km) east of Aphek (cf. v. 6). Ebenezer (meaning “stone of help”) is mentioned again in 5:1. The Ebenezer of 7:12 recalls these earlier references (7:12 note), but it is a different place, near Mizpah.

**Aphek.** Aphek was at the southern end of the plain of Sharon, about five miles (8 km) inland from the Mediterranean, near the source of the Yarkon River (29:1). It was among the cities conquered by Joshua (Josh. 12:18).

LORD **defeated us.** The elders’ question is appropriate insofar as it reflects the belief that “the battle is the LORD’s” (17:47). They do not wait for an answer, however, but immediately take matters into their own hands.

**Let us bring the ark.** The elders’ apparent conviction that the ark is a magical guarantee of the Lord’s presence is similar to that of the Philistines (vv. 7–9). This belief denies the biblical truth that salvation depends on God’s free initiative and sovereign grace, not on human techniques or schemes (2 Sam. 15:25 and note).

LORD **of hosts.** See note on 1:3.

**Hophni and Phinehas.** With his two wicked sons (2:12–17, 27–36) in charge of the ark, it is not surprising that Eli’s “heart trembled for the ark of God” (v. 13).

This word first occurs in Gen. 14:13 as a description of Abram. Extrabiblical documents of the second millennium B.C.. mention a diverse and widespread people called “Habiru.” This has caused considerable debate about whether the biblical Hebrews are the same as these people. The Habiru seem to have been a landless class of aliens or refugees who survived either by hiring themselves out as soldiers or farmers or by plundering. Although the names “Hebrew” and “Habiru” look similar, no linguistic connection exists between them.

verse_quote: mighty gods ... who struck the Egyptians.
note: The Philistines’ cry of woe betrays their polytheistic perspective but nevertheless leaves little doubt of the impact the exodus of Israel from Egypt had on surrounding nations (6:6; Josh. 2:9–11).
Far from bringing relief, the Israelites’ attempt to manipulate the Lord for their own ends results in even greater defeat (v. 2).

verse_quote: the ark of God was captured.
note:
An event as astonishing as it was disastrous, the loss of the ark surely makes “the ears ... tingle” (3:11).

**Hophni and Phinehas, died.** In fulfillment of 2:34 and 3:12.

verse_quote: clothes torn and with dirt on his head.
note: These are common signs of mourning, grief, and despair (Job 1:20; 2:12; 2 Sam. 1:2, 11).

verse_quote: his heart trembled for the ark of God.
note: Earlier rebuked for honoring his sons more than the Lord (2:29), Eli now shows a concern for the ark of God that surpasses his concern for his sons (vv. 17, 18).

Not the news of heavy losses suffered by the Israelites, nor the news of the death of his sons (v. 17), but the announcement that the ark of God has been captured prompts the reaction that results in Eli’s death.

**He had judged Israel.** There is no necessary contradiction in Eli’s being described as both priest and judge (Deut. 17:8–12; 19:17; 1 Chr. 23:2–4; 2 Chr. 19:8; Ezek. 44:15–24). “Judged” associates him with the leaders God raised up between the death of Joshua and the institution of kingship.

**forty years.** Eli’s forty-year tenure of leadership overlapped with the exploits of Samson (Judg. 13–16) and possibly also the activity of the judges mentioned in Judg. 12:8–15.

Phinehas’s wife, as she dies, names their newborn son Ichabod, meaning either “no glory” or “where is the glory?” (2:29 note). As v. 22 makes clear, the “glory” to which she refers is not primarily the house of Eli but the ark of God now lost. See also the note on 14:3.

See note on 4:1.

**Ashdod.** One of the five main Philistine cities (6:17), Ashdod is about thirty miles (48 km) south of Ebenezer and three miles (5 km) inland from the Mediterranean. Philistine occupation of Ashdod during the twelfth and eleventh centuries B.C.. is attested archaeologically. In the NT period, the site is called Azotus (Acts 8:40).

A prominent deity among the Phil­istines as well as other peoples in Mesopotamia, Syria, and Phoenicia from the middle of the third millennium B.C.., Dagon was once thought to be a fish deity because of the similarity between the name Dagon and the Hebrew word for fish (_dag_). It now appears more likely that the name is associated with the Hebrew word for grain (_dagan_), making Dagon an agricultural or fertility god. Dagon seems to have headed the Philistine pantheon (Judg. 16:23; 1 Chr. 10:10), which included the goddess Ashtoreth (31:8–10) and the god Baal-zebul (“Baal the prince”). Baal-zebul was worshiped at Ekron, and his name was intentionally distorted by the Israelites to Baal-zebub (“lord of the flies,” 2 Kin. 1:1–6, 16). The worship of Dagon is attested as late as the Maccabean period (second century B.C..).

**set it up beside Dagon.** In the ancient Near East the victorious army would carry off the gods of the vanquished and deposit them in the temple of their own gods as a sign of the inferiority and subordination of the captured gods. Though not an idol, the ark of God is treated that way by the Philistines after it is captured.
The supposedly victorious deity falls on its face doing homage to the ostensibly vanquished one (v. 2 note).

verse_quote: head ... hands were lying cut off.
note: The specific damage to the idol is to be understood in light of the common practice in antiquity of removing the head and hands of the enemy dead (Judg. 7:25; 8:6; 1 Sam. 17:54; 31:9; 2 Sam. 4:12). The same vocabulary is used of Goliath’s death at the hands of David (1 Sam. 17:48–51). What happens to the Philistine god Dagon after the ark is captured later happens to his most infamous disciple, Goliath.

Thresholds are often invested with special significance, and the practice of not stepping on the threshold of a sacred place is known, if not approved, in Israel at this time (cf. Zeph. 1:9). Linking the custom of the priests of Dagon with this humiliating incident may be intended more to ridicule them than to convey information about their ritual practice.

**to this day.** This phrase suggests a significant interval of time between the event and the account of it (cf. 6:18).

LORD **was heavy.** See v. 11 and notes on vv. 1, 4; 2:9. The Lord is not tamed by friend or foe. Refusing to be manipulated by Israel, God departs to the territory of Israel’s enemies (4:21). There He demonstrates His sovereignty, causing the Philistines to feel the weight of His hand in judgment.

**tumors.** Probably symptoms of bubonic plague, transmitted by rodents.

The reference is apparently to the rulers of the Philistine league (4:1 note), who cooperate in times of emergency.

**Gath.** The location of Gath is at modern Tel es-Safi, about twelve miles (19 km) east of Ashdod. Possibly the Philistine plan is to move the ark to another town in the hope that the plague will not break out there, showing that the plague in Ashdod has been a coincidence. This hope is dramatically dashed (v. 9).

After the failed experiment in Gath, the people of Ekron at least are no longer skeptical about the danger of keeping the ark (v. 8 note). Ekron lies nineteen miles (30 km) inland and twelve miles (19 km) northeast of Ashdod at the modern site of Tel Miqne. Of the Philistines’ major cities, it is the closest to Israelite territory during this era.
Unable to bear up under the heavy “hand of the LORD” (v. 6 note), the Ekronites now plead that the ark be returned “to its own place.”
The events recorded in the previous chapter took place not in a matter of days but months. The number seven often signifies completeness.

Together with witchcraft and sorcery (Num. 23:23), divination is explicitly condemned in Israel (Deut. 18:10, 14; Jer. 27:9; Ezek. 13:23). It is practiced by some of Israel’s neighbors at this time (Num. 22:7; Ezek. 21:21).

**What shall we do.** They have the same problem as that faced by the people of Ashdod (5:8). Moving the ark from place to place inside Philistine territory has failed, making it clear that the only solution is to return the ark to Israel.
The offering is intended to acknowledge guilt and to compensate for the offense of taking the ark (v. 4).

The procedure adopted by the Philistines has several purposes. The gold used for the models is a kind of compensation for having taken the ark (v. 4), while the images of tumors and rats are probably a form of sympathetic magic. The Philistines’ stated purpose, however, is to “give glory” to Israel’s God. With this announcement, the ark narrative comes almost full circle. Israel’s failure to honor the Lord and handle the ark properly led God to remove it from them. Now that the pagans “give glory” to the God of Israel, the ark is sent back to its people.

**your gods.** The Lord’s oppressive treatment of the gods of the Philistines is like His treatment of “the gods of Egypt” (Ex. 12:12). As the next verse indicates, this comparison is not lost on the Philistines themselves.

verse_quote: Why should you harden your hearts.
note:
Forms of the Hebrew word translated “harden” in this sentence are encountered often in the story of the rejection of the priesthood of Eli’s house and the loss of the ark. Elsewhere the word is translated “glory” (v. 5; 4:21) and “honor” (see 2:29 and note).

**dealt severely with them.** The same expression is used in 31:4; Ex. 10:2; Jer. 38:19.

An ancient Hittite ritual text shows some parallels to the procedure described here. In the Hittite ritual, relief from a plague thought to be caused by an enemy god is sought by ceremonially crowning a ram to pacify the enemy god and driving the ram down a road leading to enemy territory. In the Philistine version, the point of choosing cows that have never been yoked and of locking away their calves is apparently to make certain that if the cows do head for Israel, it will not be from natural causes or by coincidence but by the influence of Israel’s God.

Lit. “House of the Sun.” One of several places in Israel with this name, this Beth-shemesh has been identified with Tel er-Rumeileh, seven miles (11 km) east of Ekron (5:10 note). Beth-shemesh is a border city (v. 12; Josh. 15:10) frequently in dispute between the Philistines and the Israelites (2 Chr. 28:18).
Obviously not happy to be leaving their calves behind, the cows nevertheless do not deviate from their divinely directed path.
The month of June. See note on 12:17.

Although this Joshua is not mentioned elsewhere in the Bible, his field and the prominent rock located in it were apparently well known at the time the present account was written (v. 18).

**burnt offering.** See note on 10:8.

Beth-shemesh was assigned to the Levites, specifically, the descendants of Aaron (Josh. 21:16).

**set them upon the great stone.** The large rock is used as a pedestal for the ark and the gold objects, not as an impromptu altar.
See note on v. 14.

See Num. 4:5, 20. Presumptuous handling of the ark led to its capture, and a similar offense must now be purged on the occasion of its return. The problem of handling the ark improperly arises again in 2 Sam. 6.
Located nine miles (14 km) northeast of Beth-shemesh in the Sorek Valley, Kiriath-jearim is also called Kiriath-baal (Josh. 15:60; 18:14), Baalah (Josh. 15:9), and Baale-judah (2 Sam. 6:2).
LORD **.** In light of Samuel’s reference to “foreign gods” among the Israelites (v. 3), it seems that it is only at the close of these twenty years that Israel begins to seek the Lord.
LORD **... and he will deliver you.** The cycle of apostasy, oppression, repentance, and deliverance so typical of the book of Judges (Judg. 3:7–9) is repeated in the events of this chapter.
See notes on 5:2; 31:10.

A town in Benjamin seven miles (11 km) north of Jerusalem and eight miles (13 km) northeast of Kiriath-jearim, Mizpah plays a prominent role in Israel before the monarchy (10:17; Judg. 20:1; 21:1, 5, 8). It is one of the regular stops in Samuel’s circuit (v. 16). The name, meaning something like “place of watching,” implies a high vantage point and is given to a number of sites (e.g., 22:3).

verse_quote: drew water and poured it out before the
note:
LORD **.** Although this action is not paralleled elsewhere in Scripture, it seems to signify sorrow and, along with fasting, a desire to seek God earnestly (cf. 1:15; Ps. 62:8; Lam. 2:19). David’s action in 2 Sam. 23:16 occurs in a different context and has a different meaning.

**We have sinned against the** LORD **.** The words and actions (v. 4) of the Israelites give evidence of true repentance. The time is ripe for the Lord to deliver His people from their Philistine oppressors. The response of the Philistines to the convocation at Mizpah (v. 7) provides an opportunity for this deliverance.

LORD **.** In the book of Judges, “crying out” to the Lord is answered through a deliverer whom the Lord raises up (Judg. 3:9, 15). Here Samuel functions as intercessor and intermediary, while the victory is clearly the Lord’s doing (v. 10).
See note on 10:8.

LORD **thundered ... against the Philistines.** This statement dramatically recalls the earlier words of Hannah that “the adversaries ... shall be broken to pieces; against them he will thunder in heaven” (2:10; cf. 2 Sam. 22:14). Hannah’s words are immediately preceded by the statement that “not by might shall a man prevail” (2:9). Human strength is of little consequence when the Lord decides to act.
Location is unknown.

A different site than that mentioned in 4:1 (note) and 5:1, this Ebenezer nevertheless recalls the earlier episode, when the Israelites tried to manipulate their God by carrying the ark into battle only to suffer a resounding defeat. Now God has given them a great victory over the same enemies. Samuel sets up a memorial stone with the name Ebenezer, “Stone of Help,” not only to commemorate the victory but also as a reminder of the different results brought about by presumption on the one hand and by repentance on the other.

**Till now the** LORD **has helped us.** The saying means that the Lord has been with them all the way “to this place,” or “to this hour.”

verse_quote: did not again enter the territory of Israel.
note:
The reference is to the tactical situation and not to the continuing history of Israel. The Philistines have been convincingly defeated and attempt no counterattack (cf. 2 Sam. 2:28 with 3:1; also 2 Kin. 6:23 with 6:24), but this does not rule out subsequent Philistine aggression (9:16; 10:5; 13:3; 14:52).

**the hand of the** LORD **was against the Philistines.** What God did during the tenure of the ark in Philistine territory (5:4, 6; 6:5 and notes), He continues through the leadership of Samuel. Throughout Samuel’s lifetime God continues to give Israel victory, though the fighting at times is fierce (14:52). The defeat recounted in ch. 31 comes only after Samuel’s death (25:1).

Ten miles (16 km) north of Jerusalem.

**Gilgal.** Probably in the Jordan Valley near Jericho (Josh. 5:10).

**Mizpah.** See note on 7:5.

See note on 1:1. Samuel travels a yearly circuit to perform his judgeship duties. His home is Ramah, and from there he travels to Bethel, Gilgal, and Mizpah. All four of these sites are located on the main north-south road in the central hill country called “the spine.” In addition, the four towns are in a cluster, each within a twelve miles (19 km) from one another. This is one indication that the rule of the judges was more local than national.

Samuel’s sons are judges in this city, which is located about fifty miles (80 km) south of Jerusalem at Tell es-Seba. It is considered the southern border of the land of Israel. Their wicked activity is far from the authority of their father.

The reasons given by the elders for wanting a king, though acceptable in themselves (as confirmed by the narrator in vv. 1–3), are really a pretext; what they really want is to become like “all the nations” (cf. v. 20).

Since the elders couch their request in terms of a “king to judge us” (v. 5 note), Samuel initially interprets their overture as an attack on his leadership (v. 6). But the Lord points out to him that the affront is far graver than that.

**they have rejected me.** The offense of the elders’ request lies not in the concept of human kingship in itself, for kingship in Israel has long been anticipated by this point (2:10 note), but in breaking their covenant relationship with God. Their sin is to reject God as their king and to take instead a human monarch (10:19; 12:12–20; cf. Gideon’s refusal in Judg. 8:23).

verse_quote: who were asking for a king.
note: For the second time in 1 Samuel, an individual is requested. The individual given in response to the first request is Samuel (1:20 note), and it is Saul (whose name is based on the Hebrew root meaning “ask for”) who will be given in response to the second request.

verse_quote: These will be the ways of the king.
note:
Israel’s Canaanite neighbors and many of the Israelite kings were guilty of harsh practices such as those described in vv. 11–17.

**run before.** Cf. the actions of Absalom in 2 Sam. 15:1 with those of Adonijah in 1 Kin. 1:5.

**chariots.** See 2 Sam. 8:4; 15:1; 1 Kin. 4:26; 10:26–29.
See note on 22:7.
The demands of the king will either take from what belongs to the Lord (Lev. 27:30–32; Deut. 14:22, 28) or create a tax burden for his subjects.

A common verb in the book of Judges when the people of God call for divine aid because of their oppression under a foreign monarch (Judg. 3:9, 15; 4:3; 6:7; 10:10).

**your king.** See 12:13; cf. 16:1.

**the** LORD **will not answer you.** Judging by the consequences, Israel’s rejection of the Lord in favor of a human king is the moral and religious equivalent of forsaking the Lord to serve other gods (Judg. 10:10–14).

See note on v. 5.

**fight our battles.** To be contrasted with “the LORD’s battles” (18:17; 25:28).

verse_quote: Obey their voice and make them a king.
note:
The Lord’s concession to the people’s sinful request is, at this point in the account, perplexing. If their desire for a king is sinful, amounting to a rejection of God as king (vv. 7, 18 and notes), how can God grant it? One answer lies in the standards of acceptable kingship that the Lord will establish. God is graciously willing to give the people a king and even to bless him (see Deut. 17:14**–**20), although not the sort of king they envision (10:1, 7, 8 and notes). At the same time, because they adopt kingship in unbelief, they come to suffer under kings like those of the nations.

**Go every man to his city.** Samuel’s dismissal of the men of Israel implies that appointing a king will require some preparation. The course of that preparation will be related in the chapters that follow.

The opening verse of the account of Saul’s adventures is formally similar to the beginning of the birth narrative of Samuel (1:1). In both instances the father of the principal character is introduced with sufficient genealogical references to suggest a man of standing. This description is employed elsewhere in the OT to picture one who is not only wealthy but of upright character (e.g., Boaz in Ruth 2:1). In Samuel’s introduction we are also told of the father’s faithful religious observance (1:3–5), whereas in this account we are introduced immediately to Saul (v. 2), and the focus remains exclusively on external qualities.
The emphasis of this description is Saul’s physical stature and impressive appearance. Cf. the description of Absalom in 2 Sam. 14:25, 26.
Saul looks for his father’s donkeys not only in his own tribal territory of Benjamin but also in the land of Ephraim. Ephraim lies directly north of Benjamin.

verse_quote: there is a man of God in this city.
note:
A “man of God” is a prophet. That Saul is unaware of the presence and reputation of the man of God or has not thought of consulting him reflects negatively on his judgment.

**all that he says comes true.** The man of God is Samuel, of whom it is said in 3:19 that the Lord “let none of his words fall to the ground.” This is a sign that Samuel is a true prophet of the Lord (Deut. 18:21, 22).

verse_quote: there is no present to bring to the man of God.
note: The first-century historian Josephus interprets Saul’s words as a sign that he is ignorant that a true prophet will accept no reward. Israel’s writing prophets express disdain for those who prophesy for money (Mic. 3:5, 11), although there are various references to goods being offered in return for prophetic favors (e.g., 1 Kin. 14:3; 2 Kin. 4:42; 8:8). In two instances payment is explicitly refused (1 Kin. 13:7–9; 2 Kin. 5:15, 16), and in one instance where goods are accepted, the payment does not benefit the prophet personally but is distributed among the people (2 Kin. 4:42).

verse_quote: today’s “prophet” was formerly called a seer.
note: The terms are synonymous.

In the Hebrew, vv. 12, 13 convey excitement and animation as the girls urge Saul to hurry up to the city, where he will arrive just in time to meet Samuel.

**high place.** Although it was recognized that such high places (often sites of Canaanite worship) posed a clear danger to the purity of Israelite worship (e.g., Lev. 26:30; Num. 33:52; Deut. 12:2, 3; Jer. 2:20), it is apparent from passages such as this that worship of Yahweh was sometimes conducted there, especially during the early monarchy (10:5; 1 Kin. 3:2–4). After the division of the kingdom, worship at “high places” was a serious problem both in the north (1 Kin. 12:31, 32; 13:32–34) and in the south (1 Kin. 14:22–24). Removal of the high places was a major goal of reform movements under southern kings such as Hezekiah (2 Kin. 18:4) and Josiah (2 Kin. 23:5).

See note on 2:10.

**prince.** The word appears to be a title for “one designated to rule” (cf. its use with reference to Solomon as crown prince in 1 Kin. 1:35). Saul’s assignment in the immediate context is to deliver Israel from the Philistines, and against the background of ch. 8, the logical assumption is that he will go on to become king.

**Philistines.** See note on 4:1.
Saul’s failure to recognize Samuel is a troubling hint of spiritual insensitivity and inattentiveness that will increasingly characterize Saul as the narrative progresses.

verse_quote: all that is desirable in Israel.
note: This expression may suggest that Saul is just the kind of king the people want.

verse_quote: took up the leg ... set them before Saul.
note: The special treatment given Saul illustrates not only his newly elevated status but also Samuel’s divinely enabled anticipation of his arrival (vv. 15, 16). This scene is perhaps a pre-coronation banquet (see 2 Sam. 15:10–12).

Perhaps a sign of loyalty to the new king (1 Kin. 19:18; Ps. 2:12).

**anointed you to be prince.** See note on 9:16.

**his heritage.** See 9:16 (“my people Israel”); 2 Sam. 20:19 and note; Deut. 32:9. The Lord’s willingness to grant the people a human king does not mean that He forfeits His rule over Israel. The appointed king is always subordinate to God.
Samuel’s words will be confirmed to Saul as the sequence of events comes to pass in the order foretold. Finally, Saul will come under the power of the Spirit (vv. 5, 6).

The mention of a Philistine garrison foreshadows the task ahead for the one designated to deliver the people of God from the Philistines (9:16). On the stationing of garrisons in subject territories, see David’s practice in 2 Sam. 8:6.

**group of prophets.** Samuel is associated with a group of prophets in 19:20, where he is described as their leader. Note the similar association of Elisha with the “sons of the prophets” in 2 Kin. 2; 6:1; 9:1; etc. These prophetic guilds appear to have been made up of defenders of true religion in times of widespread apostasy and spiritual indifference.

**prophesying.** Prophecy in the OT is often, though not exclusively, associated with the giving of a message (see Aaron’s role as Moses’s “prophet” or spokesman in Ex. 7:1; cf. Ezek. 21:9; Amos 3:8). According to Scripture, God’s prophets are His messengers (2 Sam. 7:1–5; 12:1; 24:11, 12). In some places, prophecy is associated with music (Ex. 15:20, 21; 1 Chr. 25:1). The prophesying in view here seems to be praising God and exhorting the people with musical accompaniment.

LORD **will rush upon you.** See v. 10; note on 11:6. The activity of the Spirit with Samson is expressed in identical terms (Judg. 14:6, 19; 15:14). Whereas the Spirit is ultimately withdrawn from Saul (cf. 16:14; 18:10), David’s endowment with the Spirit is permanent (16:13). Frequently in the OT, the bestowal of the Spirit is an empowerment by God of an individual for a particular task. Conversely, God can send a lying spirit (1 Kin. 22:23) or an evil (“distressing”) spirit (16:14–16, 23; 18:10; 19:9; Judg. 9:23).

verse_quote: do what your hand finds to do.
note: In light of Saul’s general commission to deliver Israel from the Philistines (9:16) and of Samuel’s specific mention of a visible symbol of Philistine domination at the site of the third and final sign (v. 5), Samuel’s words can be taken to imply that Saul should respond to his anointing by attacking the Philistine outpost. Samuel’s words can also be interpreted as an encouragement for Saul to submit to the prophetic influence mentioned in v. 6.

verse_quote: go down before me to Gilgal.
note:
Gilgal is one of the cities on Samuel’s normal circuit (see 7:16). When Saul has done what his “hand finds to do,” he is to meet Samuel in Gilgal so that the latter can offer sacrifices and give Saul further instructions.

**burnt offerings.** A full description of the ritual of the burnt offering can be found in Lev. 1:3–17. Burnt offerings are also mentioned in 6:14, 15; 7:9, 10; 13:9, 12; 15:22; 2 Sam. 6:17, 18; 24:22–25.

**peace offerings.** The peace offering is described in Lev. 3 and is first mentioned in Ex. 20:24. Other references in Samuel to peace offerings are 11:15; 13:9; 2 Sam. 6:17, 18; 24:25.
The language is similar to Ezek. 11:19; 36:26 (cf. Jer. 31:31–34; John 3:3). But it is difficult to define Saul’s experience precisely.

verse_quote: Is Saul also among the prophets.
note: Or, “Is even Saul among the prophets?” The proverb (v. 12) expresses surprise at something highly improbable. The onlookers who know Saul are surprised to find him associating with religious enthusiasts. This question becomes proverbial in Israel when someone acts out of character (19:24).

Since the leader of a prophetic guild is sometimes called “father” (2 Kin. 2:12; 6:21), this question might be asking for the leader of this particular guild. If, on the other hand, the onlookers are contemptuous of prophecy, their surprise might be that a man of good family and social standing such as Saul is associating with such “mad fellows” (cf. 2 Kin. 9:11), whose fathers were inferior to his. Still another possibility is that the question means that the “father” or origin of the prophetic band does not follow normal rules, and Saul, unlikely as it may seem, has found a place with them. See theological note “The Prophets of God” on p. 279.
The significance of this conversation has long puzzled commentators. Some have understood Saul’s reluctance to mention the kingship (v. 16) as a sign of humility.
The Lord’s choice of Saul is now made public at Mizpah, apparently through casting a lot or using the Urim and Thummim (v. 20 and note).
Casting lots is probably the method of selection (cf. Lev. 16:8–10; Num. 26:55), and it may involve the Urim and Thummim (2:28; cf. Ex. 28:30 note; Num. 27:21; Deut. 33:8).
The Lord singles out Saul even though he is not immediately present. Something similar occurs with David (16:11).

verse_quote: rights and duties of the kingship.
note:
A similar expression in 8:9–11 refers to the negative consequences of having a king. Here it means the regulations that a king must follow (Deut. 17:14–20; 2 Kin. 11:12 note).

**laid it up before the** LORD **.** See Deut. 31:26; Josh. 24:26.

Lit. “sons of Belial”; this term was previously used of the wicked sons of Eli (2:12).

**How can this man save us.** Those who pose this question are rebels because they call into question the Lord’s process of selection.

Descended from Lot, the Ammonites were a Semitic people (Gen. 19:38; Deut. 2:19) whose kingdom was on the east side of the Jordan, south of the Jabbok River. The capital of Ammon was Rabbah, located next to a spring that feeds the Jabbok River. While Ammon was sometimes on friendly terms with Israel (2 Sam. 10:2), the Ammonites often exerted pressure on Israel’s eastern border (Judg. 3:13; 11:4–32), as the Philistines did on the west. According to the Dead Sea Scrolls and the first-century historian Josephus, the siege of Jabesh-gilead was part of a larger campaign by Nahash.

**Jabesh-gilead.** A principal city in what was probably the territory of East Manasseh, Jabesh-gilead was east of the Jordan River, twenty-two miles (35 km) south of the Sea of Chinnereth (Galilee).

verse_quote: gouge out all your right eyes.
note: While the stated reason for such treatment is to “bring disgrace on all Israel,” Josephus remarks that the loss of the right eye would have made military service impossible, since the sight of the left eye would be hindered by the shield.

verse_quote: we will give ourselves up to you.
note: While the elders of Jabesh clearly intend Nahash to understand their words as a surrender, the Hebrew verb employed is often used in the sense of soldiers “going out” to battle (8:20; 18:30; 2 Sam. 18:2–4, 6). When in v. 10 the men of Jabesh again promise to give themselves up to the Ammonites, it is with some irony because the Ammonites are still thinking of “surrender,” but the townspeople are planning to fight.

verse_quote: Spirit of God rushed upon Saul.
note: Similar language is used of the Lord’s Spirit empowering some of the judges: Othniel, Gideon, Jephthah, and Samson (Judg. 3:10; 6:34: 11:29; 13:25; 14:6, 19; 15:14).

Saul’s action roughly parallels that of the Levite in Judg. 19, and the city of Gibeah plays a central role in both episodes. The Levite’s sin was notorious, and the comparison is not at all complimentary.

**and Samuel.** See notes on 10:1, 7, 8.

Located at Khirbet Ibziq, twelve miles (19 km) west of the Jordan River, opposite of Jabesh-gilead.

**people of Israel ... men of Judah.** Even before the division of the kingdom (1 Kin. 12), a distinction is often made between the northern and southern tribes (17:52; 18:16; cf. 2 Sam. 2:10; 3:10; 5:5; 11:11; 12:8; 19:11, 40–43; 20:2; 21:2; 24:1, 9).

verse_quote: we will give ourselves up to you.
note: See note on v. 3.

See 13:17; Judg. 7:16; 9:43; 2 Sam. 18:2.

**in the morning watch.** Between 2 and 6 A.M., taking advantage of the cover of darkness.
The reference includes, but may not be limited to, the “worthless fellows” of 10:27.
LORD **has worked salvation in Israel.** Saul interrupts a question directed to Samuel with a confession that marks a high point in his own life.

verse_quote: let us go to Gilgal and there renew the kingdom.
note:
The process of Saul’s accession to the throne can now be resumed (v. 15 note), but on a deeper level it is the continued reign of the Lord that must be renewed (ch. 12).

**Gilgal.** See note on 13:4.

The rise to leadership in ancient Israel can be seen as following a three-step process: (1) designation as the Lord’s choice; (2) demonstration of valor and of having the Lord’s power through performing a heroic feat; and (3) confirmation by the people. Saul is designated by Samuel, and he has a prophetic experience (ch. 10). Although he could have attacked the Philistine garrison at Gibeah immediately (10:5, 8), he gains an important victory by delivering Jabesh-gilead (v. 13). He is then crowned at Gilgal.

**peace offerings.** See note on 10:8.

verse_quote: have made a king over you.
note: The process of accession to the throne has been completed, and Samuel’s speech in ch. 12 marks the end of the period of the judges.

Samuel advances a three-pronged argument to compel the people to recognize their guilt for requesting a king. First, he invites agreement from the people that his leadership has been blameless (vv. 4, 5). Second, he points out that in the past it was always the Lord who appointed leaders (v. 6), and these proved fully adequate (vv. 7, 8). Third, he emphasizes that even when Israel “forgot the LORD their God,” the Lord was gracious to them. Although the Lord subjected them to enemy oppression (v. 9), He heard their confessions of sin and cries for deliverance (v. 10) and raised up judges, among them Samuel himself (v. 11). Against this background of the sufficiency of the Lord’s provision, the people’s demand to have a human king, even though the Lord is their king (v. 12) can be seen for what it is (8:7). Nevertheless, kingship can succeed, if both king and people “fear the LORD and serve him and obey his voice” (v. 14).

**12:3 his anointed.** See note on 2:10. Saul’s anointing is ordered in 9:16 and performed in 10:1.

**Whose ox ... whose donkey have I taken.** Valuable possessions in biblical times, the ox and the donkey are mentioned in the tenth commandment as typical objects of covetousness (Ex. 20:17; Deut. 5:21). Samuel declares he has never taken an ox or a donkey, and this contrasts with the ways of a king (see 8:11–17).

Samuel has taken the stand himself as a defendant and been acquitted (vv. 3–5); now he takes the role of prosecutor, and the people become the defendants. Their crime is having desired a king in total disregard of all the “righteous deeds of the LORD” throughout the time of the exodus and the judges (vv. 7–11).

verse_quote: when you saw that Nahash the king of the Ammonites came against you.
note: Though it is not explicitly mentioned in ch. 8, it is possible that the Ammonite threat was already a concern at that time (11:1 note). Alternatively, Samuel may simply be citing the Ammonite episode as the most recent example of the people’s faithless tendency to seek help from men rather than God. Saul himself gave the Lord credit for the victory (11:13).

verse_quote: the king whom you have chosen.
note:
See 8:18; cf. 16:1.

**for whom you have asked.** See note on 8:10.

LORD**.** A fundamental prerequisite for covenant blessing in Moses’s day (Deut. 6:2, 24; 10:12; 31:12, 13), in Joshua’s (Josh. 4:24; 24:14), and now in the new era of the monarchy. To “fear the LORD” means standing in awe of Him and giving Him the honor and obedience that is His due as God and gracious Father.

Having made his case against the people in vv. 3–15, Samuel now invokes a dramatic sign to drive home the point of the people’s guilt. The sign achieves the desired result, and the people repent for having “added to all our sins this evil, to ask for ourselves a king” (v. 19). On signs accompanying prophetic utterances, see note on 2:34.

**12:16 stand still and see.** These two imperatives are the same commands that Moses gave to the people at the Red Sea when God divided the waters (Ex. 14:13).
The wheat harvest took place in late May and June, early in Israel’s dry season.
In response to the people’s repentance, Samuel comforts them, “Do not be afraid,” and challenges them to renewed commitment (v. 20).
Samuel’s responsibilities in the kingdom will include intercession and instruction (12:1 note; for other duties of Samuel, see 10:8).

LORD**.** See note on v. 14.

**with all your heart.** See v. 20; 16:7.

Saul’s reign officially begins. Cf. the chronological notice of 13:1 with similar formulas in 2 Sam. 2:10; 5:4; 1 Kin. 14:21; 22:42. The narrative turns to Saul’s first encounters with the Philistines, who are a continuing threat to Israel.

**13:1** Existing Hebrew manuscripts contain what is likely an inadvertent scribal departure from the original wording, since as it stands the Hebrew says that Saul was one year old when he began to rule. Saul probably reigned about twenty years, and if so, the number “forty” in Acts 13:21 is a round figure meaning “a long time.” See the chronology in Introduction: Date and Occasion.

Some four miles (6 km) northeast of Gibeah in the tribal territory of Benjamin.

**Gibeah of Benjamin.** It lies at modern Tell el-Ful in the central hill country three miles (5 km) due north of Jerusalem.

verse_quote: Jonathan defeated the garrison ... at Geba.
note:
This could be the same garrison near where Saul prophesied.

**blew the trumpet.** Trumpets were used in war as a signaling device (2 Sam. 2:28; 18:16; 20:1).

**Hebrews.** See note on 4:6.

Saul responds to the crisis precipitated by Jonathan (v. 3), gathering the people at Gilgal in accordance with Samuel’s instructions (10:8). Gilgal’s situation in the Jordan Valley near Jericho placed it outside immediate Philistine control, making it a strategic site for a general muster of the troops. Already at this point, Gilgal has figured prominently in Israel’s history (Josh. 4:19, 20; 5:10; 9:6; 10:6–15, 43; 1 Sam. 7:16; 11:14).
These are the people summoned in v. 4, not the troops already deployed in v. 2.
Samuel previously specified seven days (10:8).
See note on 10:8.

See note on 2:27–36.

**When I saw.** From a purely human perspective, Saul’s excuses seem to carry some weight. But they do not take into account the freedom of God to act on behalf of His people, as Jonathan’s testimony in 14:6 confirms.

This Hebrew expression implies both intellectual and moral failure. For a similar confrontation between a prophet and a king, see 2 Chr. 16:7–9.

**You have not kept the command.** In this context, Saul had transgressed by offering sacrifices on his own authority and usurping priestly sacrificial duties.

Saul’s hopes of establishing a dynasty are dashed, though Saul himself will not yet be deposed (15:23).

**a man after his own heart.** This phrase occurs only one other time in the OT, Deut. 20:8, which is translated “like his own heart.” In the light of passages such as 2:35 and 16:7, the text appears to be saying that David was “after God’s heart” in the sense of being committed to His will and purposes. Samuel’s God should be Saul’s God as well, but Saul has been faithless and cannot rightly say, “my God.”

Several reasons for Samuel’s reversal of his earlier decision (v. 26) may be suggested: (1) Saul has at last issued a candid confession; (2) there is no danger after vv. 28, 29 that Saul might interpret Samuel’s actions as a retraction of his judgment; (3) Samuel must still deal with Agag.

David’s rise is marked by his anointing by Samuel and his time in Saul’s service (chs. 16–18), his flight from Saul (chs. 19–23), his avoidance of bloodguilt (chs. 24–26), and his escape to the Philistines (chs. 27–31).

Cases of deception like this one must be weighed in their particular circumstances (20:6; 21:2; 27:10; 2 Sam. 16:17–19; Josh. 2:4 and notes).

verse_quote: stature, because I have rejected him.
note:
The reference to “stature” as a false measure of an individual’s qualification to be king, along with the notice that this son of Jesse is “rejected,” is reminiscent of Saul, who was notable for his height (9:2; 10:23) but was rejected (15:23, 26). verse_quote: in the midst of his brothers.
note:
It is likely that the elders also witness David’s being anointed (vv. 4, 5). The emphasis on the brothers being present at the event may shed light on Eliab’s behavior in 17:28.

**Spirit of the** LORD **rushed upon David.** See notes on 10:6; 11:6. David’s endowment with the Spirit “from that day forward” sets him apart from Saul (and also Samson) upon whom the Spirit descends only temporarily.

LORD **departed from Saul.** The empowering and validating presence of God’s Spirit must have been removed from Saul at his definitive rejection as king in ch. 15 (cf. also v. 1).

**the** LORD **is with him.** This fact, more than any human quality, accounts for David’s persistent, if circuitous, rise to power, while Saul’s increasing recognition that David is preferred to him plays no small part in his own psychological disintegration (3:19; 17:37; 18:12, 28, 29; 20:13; 2 Sam. 7:9 and notes).

verse_quote: between Socoh and Azekah, in Ephes-dammim.
note: Socoh is located at modern Khirbet ‘Abbad, fourteen miles (23 km) west of Bethlehem on the Philistine border. Azekah is identified with Tell Zakariyeh, which is three miles (5 km) northwest of Socoh, and five miles (8 km) east of the Philistine capital of Gath.
This valley runs east to west from Bethlehem to Gath through the “shephelah” or foothills, of Palestine.
