LORD **be with you, as he has been with my father.** Recognizing that David is now God’s chosen king (18:4; 23:17 and notes), Jonathan gives him allegiance over and above allegiance to his own father (v. 16).

verse_quote: do not cut off your steadfast love.
note: For the fulfillment of this request, see 2 Sam. 9:1–8; 21:7.

See note on v. 13. Since it is David himself who will be accountable to keep covenant with Jonathan, “enemies” is probably a euphemistic reference to Saul, Jonathan’s father (cf. 25:22; 2 Sam. 12:14).
See note on v. 8.
See note on v. 5.

The site is otherwise unknown. The Hebrew may mean something like “departure stone.” The stone is possibly a familiar landmark on the way out of town; for other such landmarks mentioned in Samuel, see 19:22; 2 Sam. 20:8 and notes.
LORD **is between you and me.** See Gen. 31:50, 53.
Saul’s relative and military commander (14:50).

See esp. Lev. 7:19–21; 15:16–18; Deut. 23:10, 11. Laws of cleanliness are covered most fully in Lev. 11–15, though references to “clean” and “unclean” are frequent throughout the Pentateuch (e.g., Gen. 7:2; Lev. 5:2; Num. 5:2; Deut. 14:3–21). The point is not physical but ritual or religious uncleanness.
Saul is insulting David by refusing to call him by name.
See note on v. 6., 29

verse_quote: son of a perverse, rebellious woman.
note: As in similar modern expressions, the insult is meant for Jonathan and not necessarily his mother.

verse_quote: neither you nor your kingdom shall be established.
note: Despite Samuel’s words in 13:14, Saul still clings to hope for his dynasty (cf. 18:8 note). Cf. Jonathan’s ready acceptance of the Lord’s will (v. 13; 18:4; 23:17 and notes). It may be inferred from Saul’s words that Jonathan is his firstborn and thus in line for the throne.

verse_quote: Saul hurled his spear at him.
note: Saul’s and Jonathan’s opposite reactions to David have driven a wedge between them. Saul’s attempt on Jonathan’s life matches his earlier attempts on David’s (18:11; 19:10).
The arrow travels farther than where the boy is standing, and this is a negative sign that David must run for his life (see v. 22).
See note on v. 8.

Probably located less than two miles (3.2 km) northeast of Jerusalem (Is. 10:32), Nob became “the city of the priests” (22:19) sometime after the disaster that came upon Shiloh (1:3; 2:32 and notes) at the hands of the Philistines (4:1–11).

**Ahimelech.** Either Ahijah’s brother or simply another name for Ahijah (14:3), Ahimelech occupies the position of high priest once held by his great-grandfather Eli (1:9). See also Mark 2:26 and note.
Having employed a pretext to good advantage not long before (20:6 note), David does so again, with disastrous results for Ahimelech and the priests at Nob (22:6–19).

That is, “the showbread” (v. 6; cf. Ex. 25:30; 35:13; Lev. 24:5–9; 1 Chr. 9:32). Twelve fresh loaves of bread were placed on the table in the holy place each Sabbath, and the priests were the only ones allowed to eat this bread (Lev. 24:5–9). See Jesus’ reference to this episode in Matt. 12:3, 4; Mark 2:25, 26; Luke 6:3, 4.

**kept themselves from women.** Ritual cleanliness was a part of consecration prior to battle or other important occasions (Ex. 19:15; Lev. 15:18; Deut. 23:9–14; Josh. 3:5; 2 Sam. 11:11–12).
See v. 4 and note.

The presence of Doeg at these transactions arouses apprehensions in the reader as it does in David (22:22). These apprehensions prove well founded as the narrative progresses (22:9, 10, 18, 19). Doeg is also mentioned in the title of Ps. 52.

See 17:51, 54.

**ephod.** See note on 2:28.

See 27:2–12; 29:1–11; title to Ps. 34, where “Abimelech” may be a name for Philistine kings.

**Gath.** See notes on 4:1; 5:8.

Outside as well as inside Israel, David’s royal destiny seems to be recognized, even if the Philistines’ statement is best understood as popular exaggeration.

**David his ten thousands.** See note on 18:7.

Adullam, which may mean “refuge,” is located in the foothills of Judah at the site of Khirbet ash-Sheikh about ten miles (16 km) east of Gath. See also 2 Sam. 23:13; cf. Josh. 12:15; titles to Ps. 57 and 142.

**his father’s house ... went down there to him.** The vehemence that has driven Saul to attack even his own family (20:33) leaves David’s family with little reason to feel secure.

The specific location of this city is unknown. On the name Mizpeh (“watchtower”), see note on 7:5.

**king of Moab.** Moab had a king already in Judg. 3:12.

**stay with you.** David’s decision to seek sanctuary in Moab may be based not only on the assumption that a nation at odds with Saul (14:47) might well wish to side with a rival but also on David’s family ties to the Moabites (Ruth 4:13–17).

**what God will do for me.** While taking whatever practical measures he can, David nevertheless sees God in sovereign control of his situation (2 Sam. 15:25, 26).
See note on 23:14.

Later to serve as King David’s seer (2 Sam. 24:11; 2 Chr. 29:25; cf. 1 Chr. 29:29), Gad’s presence at this point is a reminder that David’s destiny is divinely appointed and that he is under the Lord’s protection. David will later be joined by a priest (vv. 20–23).
The mention of Saul’s spear here may be a reminder of Saul’s violent temper (18:10, 11; 19:10; 20:33), which comes to full expression in this episode.

Having apparently surrounded himself with members of his own tribe (9:1, 2; 10:21), Saul seeks to reinforce their loyalty with an appeal to self-interest; he is becoming more like the kings of surrounding nations (8:12–14).

**fields and vineyards.** The questions addressed by Saul to his officials suggest that he engaged in at least some of the abusive royal practices about which Samuel had warned (8:10–18).

verse_quote: when my son makes a covenant.
note: See notes on 18:3, 4.

See 21:7 and note.

**Ahimelech the son of Ahitub.** See 21:1 and notes.

Saul’s assumption that Ahimelech has plotted with David against the king is baseless; Ahimelech was simply misled by David (21:2 note). Saul has accused the priests of Nob of conspiring against him as well (22:8).

**risen against me, to lie in wait.** Saul’s assumption of hostile motives on David’s part is as ill founded as his assumption about Ahimelech.
Ahimelech may still think at this point that David was doing covert work for Saul when he came for help (21:2).

Saul’s command that the priests of the Lord be slaughtered is so evil and irrational that his own men refuse to carry it out. At least once before, Saul’s men found it necessary to go against him (14:45 and note).

See note on 2:31.

**linen ephod.** See note on 2:18.

verse_quote: both man and woman, child and infant.
note: It is an irony extremely damaging to Saul’s image that the description of the total slaughter of the inhabitants of Nob, “the city of the priests,” matches almost verbatim the order Saul received to slaughter of the Amalekites (15:3), an order he failed to carry out.

Support for David continues to build, chiefly as a result of Saul’s misguided attempts at self-preservation. David now has the support of both prophet (v. 5) and priest. Abiathar brings to David the ephod used for discerning the Lord’s will (23:6; cf. 2:28; 14:3 and notes).

It would be easy for David to excuse himself for the massacre at Nob by simply condemning Saul. Instead, he readily admits his share of responsibility for the disaster (21:2 note). In this admission, the reader glimpses a major difference between David and his predecessor in the quality of their repentance, linked to humility (15:24–26, 30 and notes; 2 Sam. 12:13 note).

Located about three miles (5 km) south of Adullam (22:1) near Philistine territory, Keilah is also mentioned in Josh. 15:44.

**robbing the threshing floors.** Cf. Judg. 6:3–6. The primary reason for the raid is to plunder foodstores.
Not the linen ephod traditionally worn by all priests (cf. 22:18), but the ephod associated with divine inquiry (2:28 note).

verse_quote: God has given him into my hand.
note: Saul’s interpretation of events is without foundation, as the narrator’s diametrically opposed assertion makes clear: “God did not give him into his hand” (v. 14).

verse_quote: Will the men of Keilah surrender me.
note: In view of Saul’s ruthless treatment of the city of Nob, the behavior of the Keilahites probably reflects fear rather than ingratitude to David.

verse_quote: men, who were about six hundred.
note: The growth of David’s company from four hundred (22:2) to six hundred is an indication of his increasing strength (22:20 note).

The term “strongholds” (plural) suggests a geographical area, not a single location (22:4; 2 Sam. 5:17; 23:14).

**wilderness of Ziph.** The village of Ziph is thirteen miles (21 km) southeast of Keilah and five miles (8 km) southeast of Hebron. The wilderness is the desert area south of Hebron. Ziph is mentioned in Josh. 15:55, along with Maon (v. 24) and Carmel (15:12; 25:2).

**God did not give him into his hand.** God is in sovereign control of David’s destiny (v. 7; 22:20 and notes).

verse_quote: Jonathan, Saul’s son ... strengthened his hand in God.
note: No longer ignorant of his father’s malevolence toward David (cf. 20:2), Jonathan acts as a true friend by aiding David in finding strength where true strength can alone be found. See 30:6, where David once more “strengthened himself in the LORD his God.”

verse_quote: I shall be next to you.
note:
Though Jonathan will not survive to serve David (31:2), his readiness to let go of personal ambition for the sake of God’s chosen king (18:4; 20:13) is a foil to Saul’s desperate efforts to hang on to a kingdom that is no longer his (15:23).

**Saul ... knows this.** See 20:30, 31. Saul’s refusal to accept his rejection (cf. Eli’s response in 3:18) cannot be excused on the grounds that he does not know to whom the kingdom should go.
See notes on 18:3, 4.

See note on v. 14; 26:1. Ps. 54 is later penned by David in light of the Ziphites’ betrayal.

**Gibeah.** Saul’s hometown (10:26).
About eight miles (13 km) south of Hebron, Maon is mentioned in 25:2 as the hometown of Nabal.

verse_quote: Philistines have made a raid against the land.
note: The providential timing of this Philistine incursion is obvious.
Engedi is a large spring on the steep western shore of the Dead Sea. Its vicinity affords David provisions and protection in his flight from Saul.
See note on 23:29.
Saul’s elite troops.

verse_quote: Here is the day of which the
note:
LORD **said to you.** While it is providential that Saul should enter the very cave where David and his men are hidden, there has been no hint that God wants David to lift a hand against Saul (cf. v. 6). The suggestion by David’s men that he do so is a mistaken conclusion.

**cut off a corner of Saul’s robe.** David restricts himself to a symbolic act (v. 5 note). The robe symbolizes Saul’s authority as king.

Although David later displays the corner of Saul’s robe as evidence of his goodwill toward Saul (v. 11), his pangs of conscience (cf. 2 Sam. 24:10) suggest that a desire to secure such proof may not have been his only reason for going so close to Saul. In view of the royal significance of robes (15:28; 18:4; 19:24 and notes), David may have felt guilty of an inappropriate grasping after the kingship and of an act of aggression against the Lord’s anointed (v. 6).
LORD**’s anointed.** David recognizes and safeguards the sanctity of the Lord’s anointed (26:9; cf. 2:10 note), leaving judgment and vengeance to the Lord (v. 12).
David’s point seems to be like Jesus’ teaching, “You will recognize them by their fruits” (Matt. 7:16, 20). David is known by his restraint, but Saul is known from his efforts to harm David.

David abases himself before Saul, as Mephibosheth will later do before David (2 Sam. 9:8). The expression “dead dog” occurs only one other time in the OT, in 2 Sam. 16:9. “Dog” is usually an insult (17:43; 2 Sam. 3:8; 2 Kin. 8:13). This comment by David underlines his humility (see 1 Sam. 2:7, 8).

verse_quote: You are more righteous than I.
note: Having just escaped with his life, Saul experiences a rare moment of remorse. His testimony to David’s righteousness recognizes David’s right to rule; even Saul acknowledges that David did not rise to power by illicit means.

Cf. Samuel’s rebuke of Saul in 13:14: “But now your kingdom shall not continue.” Yet in contrast to Jonathan’s action in 18:4 (note), Saul gives no sign of being ready to give the throne to David (cf. 26:25 note).

The extent of mourning is a sign of Samuel’s prominence as a leader. Cf. the mourning that accompanied the deaths of Jacob (Gen. 50:10), Aaron (Num. 20:29), and Moses (Deut. 34:8).

**Ramah.** Samuel’s hometown (1:1 note).

**Paran.** A region located in the northeast Sinai Peninsula immediately to the northwest of the Gulf of Aqaba and southeast of Kadesh-barnea.

See 23:24.

**Carmel.** The same Carmel where Saul erected a monument in his own honor (15:12 notes). The setting of this incident near Carmel is the first of many reminders of Saul in this chapter. Although Carmel is a Judahite site, it seems to have political leanings toward Saul.

In v. 25 Abigail explains the name as meaning “folly.” It seems unlikely that parents would name a child “fool.” The etymological meaning of the name is probably related to an Arabic word that means “noble.” “Folly” is thus a disparaging play on a name that sounds like “fool.”

**Calebite.** Nabal is of the clan of Caleb, the trustworthy spy during the conquest who later settles in Hebron. Maon is merely eight miles (13 km) south of Hebron. On Caleb’s tribal holdings, see Josh. 14:13; 15:13. The similarity of the name “Caleb” to the Hebrew word for “dog” (cf. 24:14 note) may account for the inclusion of this particular detail in the introduction of Nabal.
Cf. the attitude of respect and deference adopted by David in addressing Saul as “my father” in 24:11.

Nabal’s attack on David’s messengers is vicious. The Hebrew verb translated “railed” means “to shriek” or “to fly at” something and is closely related to the Hebrew noun for “birds of prey.” The same verb is used of Saul in 15:19 to describe his unrestrained “pouncing” upon the Amalekite spoils (cf. 14:32).

verse_quote: They were a wall to us.
note: Not only have David’s men refrained from inflicting harm (v. 7); their presence has given protection to the shepherds of Nabal (v. 21).

verse_quote: he is such a worthless man that one cannot speak to him.
note: The designation “worthless man” is lit. “a son of Belial” (cf. 1:16; 2:12; 10:26, 27). Nabal’s plight springs from his wickedness. His lack of knowledge is a refusal to know.

verse_quote: But she did not tell her husband Nabal.
note: In refusing to confide in her husband, Abigail shows her lack of confidence in him. In view of Abigail’s insight into the Lord’s choice of David (v. 28 and note), her decision to go against her husband’s wishes seems to fall under the category of obeying God rather than men (Acts 5:29).

verse_quote: if by morning I leave ... one male.
note: Unrestrained by any special status of the man Nabal (cf. 24:9–12), David is intent upon exacting personal revenge.

Abigail calls Nabal “a son of Belial” (see note on 25:17).

**as his name is, so is he.** See note on v. 3.

Abigail’s perception of David is as right as her husband’s is wrong (vv. 10, 11; 2 Sam. 7:11–16).

**fighting the battles of the** LORD **.** Abigail’s words hint at the difference between David’s proper military role and the personal vendetta he is now pursuing. Righteous engagement in conflict means standing boldly for God and leaving personal injuries to be dealt with by the Lord (24:12).

**evil shall not be found in you.** To take his own revenge on an enemy will make David little better than Saul, and David later praises the Lord for sending Abigail to deter him from such a transgression (v. 32).
Note the poetic repetition in Abigail’s speech.

verse_quote: like the feast of a king.
note: This phrase invites the thought that Nabal is somehow like another king, Saul.

LORD **.** It would have been wrong for David to take matters into his own hands, but not because Nabal was innocent. Having heard of Nabal’s death, David thanks the Lord for keeping him from personal wrongdoing while at the same time upholding his cause.
David now has three wives: Michal, Saul’s daughter, who has been given to someone else; Ahinoam; and Abigail. See also 2 Sam. 2:2; 3:2, 3.
See note on 23:19; cf. 24:2.
See note on 2 Sam. 2:18.
See note on 24:4.
LORD**’s anointed.** See note on 24:6.
LORD **will strike him.** David’s words express an assurance gained, or at least reinforced, by the Lord’s recent dealings with Nabal (25:38, 39).
LORD **.** David’s survival and ultimate success are divinely overseen and directed (cf. 30:2, 19 and notes).

LORD **.** See note on 2 Sam. 20:19.

**Go, serve other gods.** David means that he has been expelled to live among aliens, away from the people of God.

Cf. 24:14.

**a partridge.** The partridge (Heb. “caller”) is a cleverly chosen name for David, who stands on the crest of a mountain and “calls” (vv. 13, 14).
David’s response to Saul’s confession and invitation (v. 22) indicates he doubts Saul’s sincerity; cf. Samuel’s response to a similar invitation by Saul in 15:24–26.

verse_quote: Blessed be you, my son David.
note: Saul’s behavior is erratic, and David trusts neither his confessions nor his blessings (27:1; 24:20 note).

verse_quote: one day by the hand of Saul.
note: Despite recently learned lessons of faith (26:10), David tires of being a fugitive in constant danger and gives in to the human fear that Saul will eventually succeed in destroying him. David’s anxiety may be heightened since he and his men have their families with them (v. 3). For the second time (21:10), David seeks refuge among Israel’s archenemies, the Philistines.

Now that the rift between David and Saul is conspicuous and indisputable, Achish readily accepts David’s presence, doubtless hoping to benefit from David’s allegiance in his own struggles against Saul (29:6). For the location of Gath, see 5:8.
See note on 25:40–44.

verse_quote: in the royal city with you.
note: While David’s request to be assigned to “one of the country towns” is ostensibly based on a desire not to burden the royal city, it promises him a greater freedom of action by removing him from the eyes of Achish (vv. 8–11).

Once an Israelite possession, Ziklag is under Philistine control at this time. Listed among the cities of Judah (Josh. 15:31; 19:5), ancient Ziklag may have been at Tel esh-Shariah, fifteen miles (24 km) northwest of Beersheba.

**kings of Judah.** This expression is probably from the viewpoint of a time after the division of Israel into the northern and southern kingdoms (1 Kin. 12).

Neighbors of the Philistines (Josh. 13:2), these people are not the same as the Geshurites from east of the Jordan (Josh. 13:11; 2 Sam. 15:8; 1 Chr. 2:23). David’s wife, Absalom’s mother (2 Sam. 3:3), is from the Geshurites east of the Jordan.

**Girzites.** Not identifiable; Gezer is quite distant.

**Amalekites.** See note on 15:2.

**Shur.** See note on 15:7.

verse_quote: leave neither man nor woman alive.
note: David’s practice will conceal his double-dealings from Achish (v. 11). Whether it was right is doubtful at best in the absence of any indication that the Lord has ordered his actions. This is was a partial ban in which David destroys all humans but takes other things for spoil.

This is not the first time David thinks it necessary to deceive (20:6; 21:2 and notes; cf. 16:2 note).

**the Negeb of Judah.** See 2 Sam. 24:7; 2 Chr. 28:18. The large southern region of Israel, the Negeb, extends from Beersheba south to the Gulf of Aqaba.

**Jerahmeelites.** 1 Chr. 2:9–15 mentions Jerahmeel as a descendant of Judah through Hezron and as a brother of Ram, an ancestor of David.

**Kenites.** Kenites and Jerahmeelites are mentioned together in 30:29.
Achish is deceived by David’s pretense of raiding villages in Judah and its environs.
Achish points out that his benevolence to David has certain strings attached. The same Hebrew phrase is used in Solomon’s warning to Shimei in 1 Kin. 2:37, 42.

The irony of David’s ambiguous answer (will David fight for or against him?) has a counterpoint in the perhaps unconscious irony of Achish’s reply.

**my bodyguard for life.** Presumably Achish’s offer is contingent on David’s performance in battle. The Hebrew term used by Achish for “bodyguard,” lit. “keeper of my head,” is an unfortunate choice of words in view of David’s treatment of Goliath (17:49–54). This story will resume in 29:1.

The death of Samuel signals the passing of an era.

**the mediums and the necromancers.** Although Saul’s expulsion of mediums and necromancers is fully in keeping with Mosaic law (Lev. 19:31; 20:6, 27; Deut. 18:9–14), it does not prove his personal zeal for the religion of Israel. Saul’s consultation of a medium is a clear indication of unfaithfulness and disobedience (1 Chr. 10:13); Lev. 20:6 says that such a person is to be “cut ... off from among his people.”

Located at modern Sulem in the eastern part of the Jezreel Valley. Shunem is the site of the Philistine camp on the eve of the battle in which Saul died (ch. 31).

**Gilboa.** This is probably the mountain range that begins five miles (8 km) south of Shunem and extends south along the eastern edge of the plain of Jezreel. It could also be a village located in the heart of the Gilboa range eleven miles (18 km) south of Shunem. See 29:1 and note.
See 17:11 and note.

LORD **did not answer him.** Saul’s inquiry is prompted by anxiety (v. 5), not piety, and the Lord’s refusal to answer is reminiscent of the threat of 8:18.

**by dreams, or by Urim, or by prophets.** Saul rejected the Lord and as a consequence was rejected by the Lord (15:23 and note). This has cut him off from the usual means of divine inquiry. Whereas David had the prophet Gad in his retinue (22:5), it is unlikely that a true prophet has accompanied Saul. Moreover, the authentic ephod containing the Urim and Thummim (2:28 note) has come into David’s possession through Abiathar (23:6).

verse_quote: Seek out for me a woman who is a medium.
note:
His purge of the land notwithstanding (v. 3 note), Saul seems to have no doubt that a medium can be found, and his attendants can name one immediately.

**En-dor.** Josh. 17:11, 12 attests to a persistent Canaanite influence at En-dor, which is about four miles (6 km) northeast of Shunem (v. 4 note). Saul’s recourse to En-dor takes him behind Philistine lines.

Probably this is Samuel himself, not merely an apparition. The consternation of the medium shows that the figure is something outside her usual experience of magic arts. The narrator calls it simply “Samuel,” and what the figure says is consistent with Samuel’s pronouncements when he was alive (esp. ch. 15). For some reason the Lord allows Samuel to visit Saul. It is clear from the medium’s reaction that she cannot compel him to appear.

verse_quote: Saul knew that it was Samuel.
note: Apparently Saul recognizes Samuel when the woman describes his mantle. Robes have symbolized the fate of Saul’s kingship in a variety of ways, and mention of Samuel’s mantle recollects the devastating pronouncement of 15:28 (see also 18:4; 24:4–6).
Saul’s egotism is on display in this verse: he uses the first-person pronoun six times in his response to Samuel.

verse_quote: you and your sons shall be with me.
note: That is, among the dead (31:2–4).
See note on 1:7.

Much has changed since Saul’s first encounter with Samuel, when he was designated as the one to deliver Israel from the Philistines (9:16) and was treated to a festal meal by the prophet (9:22–24). Now in his last encounter with Samuel, on the eve of his own death and the crushing Philistine defeat of Israel, Saul is treated to a fatted calf by a medium.

This notice resumes the account initiated in 28:1, 2 but suspended in order to relate Saul’s visit with the medium (28:3–25).

**Aphek.** Probably the same Aphek mentioned in 4:1 (note), twenty-eight miles (45 km) north of Gath. The Philistines assemble their forces at Aphek before continuing their northward march (v. 2). The site is located on the main highway called the “Great Trunk Road.”

**Jezreel.** North of Mount Gilboa, a few miles south of Shunem, and forty miles (64 km) northeast of Aphek.

See note on 4:6.

**I have found no fault in him.** This judgment is a measure of Achish’s gullibility, not David’s sincerity (27:8–12).

verse_quote: lest in the battle he become an adversary.
note: The other Philistine commanders are less gullible than Achish and perhaps still carry painful memories of mid-battle defection in an earlier war with Israel (14:21).

verse_quote: Is not this David, of whom they sing.
note: See note on 18:7; 21:11. Apparently this song is famously known even in Philistia.

A protest of genuine innocence when spoken to Saul (26:18), the question is now no more than a ruse. David has indeed done much (27:8–12)—if Achish is willing to see it.

**that I may not go and fight against the enemies of my lord the king.** As in 28:2, David deals in ambiguities apparent to the reader, if not to Achish. The ambiguity here is the identity of “my lord the king.” It could be Achish, Saul, or possibly God Himself.

verse_quote: you are as blameless in my sight as an angel of God.
note: Achish’s grossly misplaced confidence makes him appear practically a fool. On the expression “angel of God,” see 2 Sam. 14:17, 20; 19:27.

See note on 27:6.

**Amalekites had made a raid.** See notes on 15:2, 8. Having been the victims of David’s forays (27:8), the Amalekites have taken the opportunity of David’s absence from Ziklag to retaliate.

**the Negeb.** See note on 27:10.
A remarkable evidence of the Lord’s providential protection of David (v. 19; 26:12), whose own practice has been quite different (27:9).

verse_quote: their wives and sons and daughters taken captive.
note: This turn of events is especially troubling, inasmuch as concern for the safety of their families may have motivated the retreat of David and his men to Philistine territory in the first place (27:1 note).
LORD **his God.** See note on 23:16.
See note on 22:20.

Seasonal rivers (or wadis) from the vicinity of Beersheba and south converge to form the brook Besor, which runs northwest to empty into the Mediterranean. David and his men have come to the ravine some thirteen miles (21 km) south of Ziklag.
Their exhaustion is not surprising after a march of more than sixty miles (nearly 100 km) from Aphek (29:1–11) to the brook Besor.

The Cherethites were probably from Crete. They are often mentioned alongside the Philistines (Ezek. 25:16; Zeph. 2:5). The “Cherethites and Pelethites” served under the command of Benaiah, son of Jehoiada, as professional troops loyal to David (2 Sam. 8:18; 15:18; 20:7, 23) and, for a short time at least, to Solomon (1 Kin. 1:44). They seem to have been the king’s bodyguard (2 Sam. 23:20, 23).

**the Negeb of Caleb.** Caleb, son of Jephunneh, is first mentioned in Num. 13:6 as one of the spies chosen to scout out the land of Canaan. He is commended in Num. 14:24 as one who followed the Lord “fully” and who therefore would receive an inheritance in the Promised Land. His inheritance included Hebron (Josh. 14:13, 14; Judg. 1:20).
This is further, striking evidence of the Lord’s watchful care over David’s affairs (v. 2 note).
See note on v. 9.
See note on 2:12, where the same Hebrew expression is used.

LORD **has given us.** David recognizes that the successful rescue is not his doing but the Lord’s (vv. 2, 19 and notes). This leads him to reject the idea that the frontline troops have a right to more spoil than those who stayed behind.

verse_quote: spoil to ... the elders of Judah.
note: Probably he is thanking them for the help he received in escaping from Saul (v. 31), though it is also in this area that David’s kingship is first officially recognized (2 Sam. 2:1–4).

As v. 31 says, these cities are within the range of David’s roamings as a fugitive. All of them are in the south of Judah. This Bethel (v. 27) should not be confused with the more northern city of the same name (7:16 note).
See note on 28:4.

verse_quote: Jonathan and Abinadab and Malchi-shua, the sons of Saul.
note: See 14:49. For a listing of all four sons of Saul, see 1 Chr. 8:33. Only one of Saul’s sons remains alive after the battle (see 2 Sam. 2:8).

See note on 14:6.

**Saul took his own sword and fell upon it.** While some praise Saul’s action as worthy of a tragic hero, the tenor of the books of Samuel points in another direction. To be commended are those who, like David, in times of distress find strength in God (23:16; 30:6), and who, like Jonathan, yield fully to His will (18:4, 28, 29; 19:4; 20:31; 23:17 and notes).
On the qualified sense of “all,” see note on 15:8.

**Beth-shan.** Located in the Jordan Valley some sixteen miles (26 km) south of the Sea of Chinnereth (Galilee), this border city of the territory of Manasseh is listed in Josh. 17:11, 16; Judg. 1:27 among those cities that resisted Israelite occupation and remained Canaanite and Philistine strongholds.
